q: Of all the proposals reviewed by Ali at the clinic, this one is the _____.
e: A comparison with all members of a group requires the superlative form.

q: At the museum, Zara said this notice was _____ than the previous one.
e: A comparison between two items requires the comparative form.

q: For Ali's work at the office, this is _____ the most practical report.
e: “By far” can intensify a superlative.

q: According to Ali's letter, the two routes to the clinic are _____ safe.
e: An adverb is needed to modify the adjective “safe.”

q: At the station, Ali completed the letter _____.
e: An adverb modifies the verb phrase “completed the task.”

q: At the clinic, Sana, the manager responsible for the notice, was _____ surprised by the result.
e: “Quite” is an adverb of degree; “quiet” has a different grammatical function and meaning.

q: While Ali waited near the office, the train arrived _____ late.
e: An adverb is required to modify the adjective/adverb “late.”

q: Choose the usual position of the frequency adverb in Hira's sentence about the museum.
o: Hira visits the museum often always.
e: A frequency adverb such as “often” normally comes before the main verb.

q: On Iqra's article at the garden, the second team worked _____ than the first.
e: The comparative adverb “more efficiently” compares how two teams worked.

q: Choose the sentence with correct adverb placement in the account of Ali's letter.
o: Ali never has missed a deadline.
Ali has never missed a deadline.
Never Ali has missed a deadline.
Ali has missed never a deadline.
e: With an auxiliary verb,“never” normally follows the first auxiliary.

q: Of the three candidates assessed by Ali at the clinic, the final candidate answered _____.
e: The superlative adverb compares the manner of answering among three candidates.

q: At the library, Ali spoke _____ enough for everyone to hear the announcement about the summary.
e: The adverb “loudly” modifies the verb “spoke.”

q: For Mehak's session at the office, neither the teacher nor the students _____ ready with the plan.
e: With neither...nor, the verb normally agrees with the nearer subject,“students.”

q: During Fahad's visit to the station, neither the students nor the teacher _____ ready with the plan.
e: The nearer subject “teacher” is singular, so the singular verb is used.

q: For Talha, ten kilometres from the library _____ a long distance to walk while carrying the plan.
e: A measurement viewed as one amount takes a singular verb.

q: In Nadia's plan for the museum, there _____ several reasons for the delay.
e: In a there-construction, the verb agrees with the following plural noun phrase “several reasons.”

q: Outside the museum, a number of applicants for Noor's programme _____ waiting with the plan.
e: “A number of + plural noun” takes a plural verb.

q: At the museum, each of Hira's students _____ a copy of the plan.
e: “Each” is singular and takes the singular verb “has.”

q: According to Omar's plan at the garden, the number of applicants _____ increased.
e: “The number of” refers to one total and therefore takes a singular verb.

q: The news in Fahad's plan from the library _____ encouraging today.
e: “News” ends in -s but is grammatically singular.

q: For Sana at the library, bread and butter _____ the usual breakfast before working on the plan.
e: Two nouns expressing one customary dish or unit may take a singular verb.

q: On Omar's desk at the garden, the list of required documents _____ beside the plan.
e: The head of the subject phrase is the singular noun “list,” not “documents.”

q: Water _____ at 100°C at sea level.
e: The present simple states a general scientific fact.

q: I _____ what you mean.
e: Stative verbs such as “understand” are not normally used in the continuous for a present state.

q: This is the first time I _____ this software.
e: “This is the first time...” is normally followed by the present perfect.

q: How long _____ you _____ here?
e: A situation extending up to the present commonly takes the present perfect.

q: Sara _____ already _____ the notice.
e: The present perfect uses has/have + past participle for a completed action linked to the present.

q: Ali _____ on the letter since morning.
e: The present perfect continuous expresses an activity continuing from the past to the present.

q: Look! Sana _____ the letter now.
e: The present continuous describes an action happening now.
